<div class="refresher-question" data-question="1">

### Question 1 · What is selected?

Read the second line in words. How many trait columns will it retain? Why should an isolate ID stay outside this numeric trait matrix?

```{r refresh-columns, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
trait_names <- c("extension", "melanin", "enz_cel", "spore_abund")
trait_data <- fungi[, trait_names]
```

<details class="answer"><summary>Reveal answer: observations and variables</summary>

Keep all rows and the four named trait columns. The comma separates row and column selection. An ID identifies an isolate; even a numeric-looking ID is not a measured trait and should not influence trait distances or a PCA. Different traits from one isolate do not create additional independent isolates.

</details>
</div>

<div class="refresher-question" data-question="2">

### Question 2 · Keep rows aligned

What does `keep` contain? Why use the same selection for both objects?

```{r refresh-complete, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
keep <- complete.cases(trait_data)
fungi_complete <- fungi[keep, ]
trait_matrix <- trait_data[keep, ]
```

<details class="answer"><summary>Reveal answer: one logical selection</summary>

`keep` is a logical vector: `TRUE` where all selected trait values are observed. Applying it to both objects keeps measurements and metadata in matching order. It does not replace missing values or guarantee that the retained sample represents the excluded isolates. On Day 3, we retained 28 of 31 records.

</details>
</div>

<div class="refresher-question" data-question="3">

### Question 3 · What did scale() do?

What do you expect from the second line? Does a standardised value of `+1` mean one extra raw measurement unit?

```{r refresh-scale, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
trait_scaled <- scale(trait_matrix)
round(colMeans(trait_scaled), 6)
```

<details class="answer"><summary>Reveal answer: standardisation</summary>

The column means should round to zero. Each column was centred and divided by its sample SD. `+1` means one SD above that trait's mean in the retained sample, not one raw unit. Standardising does not make data normally distributed. Today we will retain soil responses in their original units so that mean differences and slopes remain directly interpretable.

</details>
</div>

<div class="refresher-question" data-question="4">

### Question 4 · Two parts of a PCA result

Which command gives coordinates of isolates, and which gives trait weights? What does `[, 1:2]` select?

```{r refresh-extract, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
pca_result$x[, 1:2]
pca_result$rotation[, 1:2]
```

<details class="answer"><summary>Reveal answer: extract the right result</summary>

`$x` contains isolate scores; `$rotation` contains trait loadings. Both selections keep all rows and the first two columns. `$` accesses a named part of an analysis result. Today `coef()`, `confint()` and `summary()` will help us access parts of fitted models.

</details>
</div>

<div class="refresher-question" data-question="5">

### Question 5 · What do the group numbers mean?

What does this request? Is group 3 necessarily more stress-tolerant than group 1?

```{r refresh-cluster, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
groups <- cutree(cluster_tree, k = 3)
table(groups)
```

<details class="answer"><summary>Reveal answer: labels and counts</summary>

Cut the tree into three groups and count their members. Cluster numbers are arbitrary labels, not rankings of ecological performance. Asking for three groups does not prove that three natural strategies exist. Today our treatment groups are defined by the experiment, rather than created by a clustering algorithm.

</details>
</div>

<div class="refresher-question" data-question="6">

### Question 6 · Extract and save a figure

The object `pca_plot` has been created. What kind of file does this save? Does saving the picture also save the commands and data needed to reproduce it?

```{r refresh-save, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
ggsave("Day3_PCA.png", plot = pca_plot,
       width = 7.5, height = 5.5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

<details class="answer"><summary>Reveal answer: figure versus workflow</summary>

It saves a PNG image, with the specified dimensions in inches by default and resolution in dots per inch. The image does not save the analysis workflow. Keep the original data and an R script that imports, prepares, analyses and plots them. Restart R and rerun the script to check reproducibility.

</details>
</div>

## 1. Two ecological questions, two predictor types {#question}

**Together · 10 minutes.** We return to the familiar soil microcosm dataset. A row records one soil experimental unit. The measured columns do not create extra independent replicates. Our two analyses use different subsets and different responses:

| Analysis | Ecological question | Response | Predictor |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **A · Compare groups** | How does mean aggregate stability differ among control, drought, herbicide and salinity treatments? | `WSA`, a proportion | A categorical treatment label |
| **B · Describe a trend** | Among mixtures of 2, 5 and 8 factors, how is litter mass loss associated with factor count? | `Decom`, a proportion | `Lv`, a numerical count |

`WSA` is water-stable aggregate proportion. `Decom` is proportional tea litter dry mass loss over the incubation, not a measured daily decomposition rate. For either response, a difference of `0.10` means **10 percentage points**. Do not automatically apply that conversion to other variables such as soil pH.

**Do:** write one prediction and ecological reason for each question as comments in your script. Identify the experimental unit and explain what about the design would support treating units as independent. A plot or statistical test cannot establish independence by itself.

### One modelling language

R formulas follow **`response ~ explanatory_variable`**:

- `WSA ~ treatment` estimates a separate mean for each treatment category.
- `Decom ~ Lv` estimates a straight-line mean trend across numerical factor counts.

Both are **linear models**. The one-way ANOVA is a way to examine a linear model with one categorical predictor; `aov()` provides a convenient ANOVA interface. This lesson uses ordinary linear models. Generalized linear models with other response distributions and link functions are a separate topic.

## 2. Inspect four treatment groups {#data}

**Purpose:** see the observations and confirm the comparison before fitting a model.

Extract the student files, open `ABV_Day4.Rproj`, and save the starter script as `Day4_yourname.R`. Load `ggplot2`, which you used on earlier days. If it is missing, run `install.packages("ggplot2")` once in the Console.

We select four explicitly named treatment labels: **CT = control, D = drought, H = herbicide, S = salinity**. These are four teaching groups, chosen to keep the analysis manageable, not all treatments in the study. Labels such as `"2"` describe mixtures and are not included here. Choosing `Lv == 1` alone would also include additional rows labelled `"1"` in this course file.

```{r import-groups}
library(ggplot2)
file.exists("MultiFactor_data.csv")
soil_data <- read.csv("MultiFactor_data.csv")
dim(soil_data)

group_codes <- c("CT", "D", "H", "S")
group_raw <- soil_data[soil_data$remark %in% group_codes, ]
group_raw$treatment <- factor(
  group_raw$remark,
  levels = group_codes,
  labels = c("Control", "Drought", "Herbicide", "Salinity")
)
table(group_raw$treatment)
sum(is.na(group_raw$WSA))

group_excluded_ids <- group_raw$X[is.na(group_raw$WSA)]
group_data <- group_raw[!is.na(group_raw$WSA), ]
rownames(group_data) <- paste0("record_", group_data$X)
```

`%in%` means “matches any of these values.” `factor()` tells R that these are categories and fixes their order. Our first level, Control, is the reference category when inspecting coefficients later. We exclude missing **WSA**, rather than removing a unit because an unrelated enzyme measurement is missing.

```{r group-summaries}
group_counts <- table(group_data$treatment)
group_means <- aggregate(WSA ~ treatment, data = group_data, FUN = mean)
group_sds <- aggregate(WSA ~ treatment, data = group_data, FUN = sd)
group_summary <- data.frame(
  treatment = levels(group_data$treatment),
  n = as.integer(group_counts),
  mean_WSA = group_means$WSA,
  SD_WSA = group_sds$WSA
)
group_summary
```

Use the supplied figure recipe to show **every observation**, group spreads, and means. Points are moved slightly sideways for readability; their WSA values are unchanged. The diamond marks each group mean. The box's centre line is its **median**, which need not equal the mean.

```{r group-plot}
group_plot <- ggplot(group_data, aes(x = treatment, y = WSA)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA, fill = "#edf3e7") +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, seed = 4),
             alpha = 0.8, colour = "#245e49", size = 2.2) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 18, size = 4, colour = "#a56424") +
  labs(x = "Treatment applied alone", y = "Water-stable aggregate proportion",
       title = "Aggregate stability in four soil treatments",
       subtitle = "Each circle = one soil unit; diamond = group mean") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
group_plot
```

**Do:** record each group's sample size. Describe two visible features, including a difference in spread or overlap. Keep the descriptions separate from any test conclusion.

<details class="answer"><summary>Check: counts, means and reference figure</summary>

The full CSV has **353 rows and 23 columns**. The selected groups contain **20 control, 7 drought, 8 herbicide and 10 salinity** units: **45 units total**, with **no missing WSA** in this selection. Mean WSA is approximately **0.606, 0.462, 0.610 and 0.467**, respectively.

```{r reference-groups, echo=FALSE, fig.show='asis', fig.width=7.5, fig.height=5, fig.alt='All 45 WSA observations across control, drought, herbicide and salinity. Drought and salinity means are lower, with variation within all groups.', purl=FALSE}
print(group_plot)
```

Drought and salinity have lower sample means than control; the herbicide mean is close to the control mean. Groups overlap and their spreads differ. Visual overlap alone does not answer a population-mean comparison. `outlier.shape = NA` hides duplicate boxplot symbols; **all observations remain present as circles and remain in the analysis**.

</details>

<label class="step-check"><input type="checkbox" data-step="data"> I checked the selected units, response-specific missingness, and raw group patterns.</label>

## 3. Fit and check the group model {#model}

**Purpose:** understand what is fitted and whether its assumptions deserve concern.

```{r fit-group-model}
group_model <- aov(WSA ~ treatment, data = group_data)
head(fitted(group_model))
head(residuals(group_model))
```

This model predicts each unit using its treatment group's mean. A **residual** is **observed WSA − fitted WSA**: the variation left around that mean. We fit the model to obtain residuals, inspect it, and then interpret its tests.

### Check the design and two diagnostic plots

For ordinary ANOVA inference we need independent errors, a suitable model for group means, approximately common error variance, and an adequate normal-error approximation. The whole pooled response does not have to form one normal distribution. Small, unequal groups make unusual observations and unequal variances worth examining carefully.

```{r group-diagnostics}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(group_model, which = 1)
plot(group_model, which = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Use this checklist:

| Check | What to look for | What it cannot establish |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Design | Distinct independently assigned/handled soil units; consider shared blocks or batches | A residual plot cannot prove independence. |
| Residuals versus fitted | Compare vertical spread around each fitted group mean; note unusually large residuals | Four vertical bands are expected because there are four fitted means. |
| Normal Q-Q plot | Broadly straight pattern; inspect strong tail departures | Exact alignment is not expected, and a plot is not a certificate of validity. |

**Do:** write one sentence about spread, one about tails or unusual observations, and one about independence. Use the raw data plot alongside the residual plots.

<details class="answer"><summary>Check: discuss concerns without deleting observations</summary>

```{r reference-group-diagnostics, echo=FALSE, fig.show='asis', fig.width=9, fig.height=4.2, fig.alt='Residual-versus-fitted and normal Q-Q diagnostics for the four-group WSA model.', purl=FALSE}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(group_model, which = 1)
plot(group_model, which = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The sample SDs are approximately **0.073, 0.099, 0.120 and 0.101**. Their inequality and the unequal sample sizes deserve attention; neither immediately invalidates the fit nor proves the common-variance assumption adequate. Describe what you see and discuss how it could affect uncertainty.

Labels identify observations for investigation, not automatic deletion. Check transcription, measurement records and design; retain legitimate observations even when they make a diagnostic plot less tidy. A Shapiro p-value alone should not trigger an automatic switch of analysis. A rank-based test would also answer a different question and needs its own assumptions.

For the required exercise, we continue with the classical model **as a conditional analysis**. The optional Welch check explores sensitivity to the common-variance assumption. If diagnostics or design raise major concerns in your own data, revise the analysis with guidance rather than treating today's code as an automatic recipe.

</details>

<label class="step-check"><input type="checkbox" data-step="model"> I can explain a residual and have recorded design and diagnostic concerns.</label>

## 4. Ask an overall question, then compare pairs {#compare}

**Purpose:** distinguish “some means differ” from “this pair differs,” while accounting for multiple comparisons.

### A. The overall ANOVA

Our null hypothesis is **all four population mean WSA values are equal**. The alternative is that at least one differs. ANOVA compares variation among fitted group means with variation remaining within groups.

```{r overall-anova}
summary(group_model)
```

Find the treatment row, its F statistic, and `Pr(>F)`. Under the null model and its assumptions, the p-value measures how unusual an F statistic at least this large would be. It does not measure the probability that all means are equal or the size of an ecological effect.

<details class="answer"><summary>Check: what the overall result supports</summary>

For this selection, **F(3, 41) ≈ 8.25, p ≈ 0.000207**. Under the model assumptions, the data provide evidence against a common mean across these four groups. This does **not** establish that every treatment differs from control, identify the differing pairs, or demonstrate ecological importance.

</details>

### B. Six comparisons form one family

Four groups give **six pairwise comparisons**. If we examine all six, separate unadjusted tests can increase the chance of at least one false positive. We use **Tukey comparisons** for this planned family. They provide mean differences, simultaneous confidence intervals, and adjusted p-values under the common-variance model.

```{r tukey-comparisons}
tukey_result <- TukeyHSD(group_model, conf.level = 0.95)
tukey_result

pairwise_table <- data.frame(
  comparison = rownames(tukey_result$treatment),
  tukey_result$treatment,
  row.names = NULL,
  check.names = FALSE
)
pairwise_table
```

Read each label as **first group minus second group**. For example, `Drought-Control` has the same direction as Day 2. The table columns are:

- **`diff`**: estimated mean difference in WSA proportion;
- **`lwr`, `upr`**: lower and upper limits of the Tukey interval;
- **`p adj`**: p-value adjusted for the family of six pairwise comparisons.

We can focus our written report on the three control comparisons **while retaining the six-pair adjustment**:

```{r control-comparisons}
control_comparisons <- pairwise_table[
  pairwise_table$comparison %in% c("Drought-Control", "Herbicide-Control", "Salinity-Control"),
]
control_comparisons
```

**Your task:** explain all three control comparisons using their estimated difference, interval and ecological units. Which interval includes zero? Why does that not demonstrate equal soil functioning?

<details class="answer"><summary>Check: magnitude, uncertainty and ecological meaning</summary>

| Comparison | Difference in percentage points | Approximate Tukey 95% limits, percentage points | Adjusted p |
|:---|---:|:---|---:|
| Drought − Control | −14.4 | −25.4 to −3.5 | 0.0055 |
| Herbicide − Control | +0.4 | −10.0 to +10.8 | 0.9996 |
| Salinity − Control | −13.9 | −23.5 to −4.2 | 0.0022 |

Under the fitted model, drought and salinity have lower mean WSA than control, with intervals excluding zero. The herbicide estimate is close to zero, but its interval still permits differences in either direction that could matter ecologically. A large p-value does not establish equivalence; a suitable equivalence margin and analysis would be needed for that question.

To judge ecological importance, connect aggregate stability to relevant processes such as erosion resistance or water movement, compare the magnitude with natural variation and measurement precision, and consider persistence under field conditions. Statistical significance alone does not answer this.

The drought mean difference matches Day 2. Its interval and p-value differ because today's model pools an error variance across four groups and adjusts a six-pair comparison family; Day 2 used a two-group Welch test. Do not expect a simple numerical conversion between the two methods.

</details>

<details class="plan"><summary>Reference figure: all six differences with intervals</summary>

```{r reference-comparisons, echo=FALSE, fig.show='asis', fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5, fig.alt='Six pairwise WSA mean differences with Tukey simultaneous intervals, displayed in percentage points and compared with zero.', purl=FALSE}
ggplot(pairwise_table, aes(x = 100 * diff, y = comparison)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey55") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 100 * lwr, xend = 100 * upr, yend = comparison), colour = "#6a8f62") +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#245e49") +
  labs(x = "WSA difference (percentage points)", y = NULL,
       title = "One comparison family: all six pairs",
       subtitle = "Tukey 95% simultaneous intervals; first group minus second") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

</details>

<label class="step-check"><input type="checkbox" data-step="compare"> I distinguished the overall test from pairwise estimates and explained the adjustment family.</label>

<div class="break-note">Break · Save your script and take 10 minutes. Before continuing, explain why a categorical treatment and a numerical factor count are different predictors.</div>

## 5. Fit a numerical trend among factor mixtures {#regression}

**Purpose:** use a slope to describe how a response varies with a numerical predictor.

We now switch question, response and data subset. **Among mixtures of 2, 5 and 8 factors, how is proportional litter mass loss associated with factor count?** This regression uses neither the four-group WSA response nor an unlabelled combination of all rows.

At each count, different soil units received **different factor combinations**. This lets us describe a broad association across the supplied mixtures, but a count alone does not identify which factors were present or separate their contributions. This simple exercise does not reproduce the paper's full causal or predictive analysis.

### Select and count the observations

```{r regression-data}
mixture_raw <- soil_data[soil_data$Lv %in% c(2, 5, 8), ]
table(mixture_raw$Lv)

reg_keep <- complete.cases(mixture_raw[, c("Decom", "Lv")])
reg_excluded_ids <- mixture_raw$X[!reg_keep]
regression_data <- mixture_raw[reg_keep, ]
rownames(regression_data) <- paste0("record_", regression_data$X)

nrow(regression_data)
table(regression_data$Lv)
reg_excluded_ids
str(regression_data[, c("Decom", "Lv")])
```

**Do:** record candidate and retained sample sizes, missing-response exclusions, and observed factor counts. Check that `Lv` is numerical rather than a factor. Keep other columns for context, but do not remove records because an unused variable is missing.

<details class="answer"><summary>Check: a different analysis population</summary>

There are **147 candidate mixture units**: 47 with 2 factors, 50 with 5, and 50 with 8. Six lack `Decom`, leaving **141 observed units**: **45, 49 and 47**, respectively. The excluded record IDs in column `X` are **229, 251, 297, 344, 349 and 356**.

Different units within one count have different factor identities. They are not replicate measurements of one identical mixture. Our conclusions concern this selected set of mixtures and the fitted model, not a universal effect of adding any factor to any soil.

</details>

### Fit a straight line

```{r fit-regression}
trend_model <- lm(Decom ~ Lv, data = regression_data)
summary(trend_model)
coef(trend_model)
confint(trend_model)
```

Read the model as **fitted mean mass-loss proportion = intercept + slope × factor count**. The intercept and slope describe a straight-line summary. The numerical `Lv` term assumes the same mean change per additional factor across this range. That assumption is something to assess, not a fact established by typing the formula.

```{r regression-plot}
trend_plot <- ggplot(regression_data, aes(x = Lv, y = Decom)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.10, height = 0, seed = 4),
             colour = "#245e49", alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE,
              colour = "#a56424", fill = "#e6d4b9") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2, 5, 8)) +
  labs(x = "Number of applied factors", y = "Proportional litter mass loss",
       title = "A straight-line summary across factor mixtures",
       subtitle = "141 observed units; points jittered horizontally only") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
trend_plot
```

**Do:** describe the fitted direction and the variation around the line. Are observations available at every integer count between 2 and 8? Does the shaded band contain the middle 95% of individual observations?

<details class="answer"><summary>Check: line, observations and the shaded band</summary>

```{r reference-trend, echo=FALSE, fig.show='asis', fig.width=7.5, fig.height=5.2, fig.alt='Litter mass-loss observations at factor counts 2, 5 and 8, with a descending fitted regression line and model-based confidence band for the mean response. Scatter increases at higher counts.', purl=FALSE}
print(trend_plot)
```

The fitted line slopes down, while many observations differ substantially from it. We observed only **2, 5 and 8 factors**; points appear slightly to either side because of plotting jitter. There are no observed 3-, 4-, 6- or 7-factor groups in this subset.

The shaded band is the ordinary model's approximate **95% confidence band for the mean response at each predictor value**, not an interval containing 95% of individual observations or a simultaneous guarantee for the whole line. Its calibration depends on the model assumptions. An interval for a new individual soil unit would answer a different question and is usually wider.

</details>

<label class="step-check"><input type="checkbox" data-step="regression"> I selected the mixture data, fitted a numerical trend and distinguished a mean-response band from individual variation.</label>

## 6. Interpret the line and examine what it misses {#interpret}

**Purpose:** report an understandable association and judge the limits of its uncertainty estimates.

### Three quantities to read

Use these commands to isolate the slope, its ordinary confidence interval, and R-squared:

```{r regression-summary}
slope <- coef(trend_model)["Lv"]
slope_interval <- confint(trend_model)["Lv", ]
r_squared <- summary(trend_model)$r.squared

slope
100 * slope
slope_interval
r_squared
```

| Quantity | Meaning here | Avoid this interpretation |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Slope | Fitted change in mean mass-loss proportion per additional factor under a straight-line model | The effect of adding any particular factor to any mixture. |
| Slope CI | Model-based uncertainty about that slope | A range containing most individual observations, or proof of a mechanism. |
| R-squared | Fraction of observed response variation accounted for by this fitted line in these data | Forecast accuracy for new data, or the fraction of soil functioning caused by factor count. |

**Your task:** convert the slope into percentage points per additional factor. Explain why the intercept is not an estimated mean for the measured control units in this analysis.

<details class="answer"><summary>Check: a possible slope interpretation</summary>

The fitted slope is approximately **−0.00745 proportion per factor**, or **−0.745 percentage points of litter mass loss per additional factor** under this straight-line summary. Its ordinary 95% interval is approximately **−0.01114 to −0.00376** proportion per factor (**−1.114 to −0.376 percentage points**).

The line accounts for about **10.3%** of the observed variation (`R² ≈ 0.103`). Most variation remains around the line. The summary's small slope p-value is also conditional on the fitted mean and error assumptions; it does not remove the diagnostic concerns below.

The intercept corresponds to `Lv = 0`, outside this subset's observed range of 2–8. It is part of the line equation, not an observed control mean and not an invitation to extrapolate. A negative fitted association does not isolate the causal contribution of factor count from changing factor identities and combinations.

</details>

### Check the mean pattern and residual spread

```{r regression-diagnostics}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(trend_model, which = 1)
plot(trend_model, which = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

mixture_means <- aggregate(Decom ~ Lv, data = regression_data, FUN = mean)
mixture_sds <- aggregate(Decom ~ Lv, data = regression_data, FUN = sd)
mixture_means
mixture_sds
```

**Discuss together:** is the response spread similar at each factor count? Does a straight line follow the three observed means closely? What consequences could these patterns have for the usual confidence intervals?

<details class="answer"><summary>Check: the real data reveal model limitations</summary>

```{r reference-regression-diagnostics, echo=FALSE, fig.show='asis', fig.width=9, fig.height=4.2, fig.alt='Regression residual-versus-fitted and Q-Q plots, showing changing residual spread and tail departures that warrant caution about ordinary model inference.', purl=FALSE}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(trend_model, which = 1)
plot(trend_model, which = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Observed SDs are approximately **0.031, 0.053 and 0.068** at 2, 5 and 8 factors. The larger spread at higher counts raises a **nonconstant-variance** concern. Means are approximately **0.652, 0.650 and 0.608**: the 2- and 5-factor means are similar, followed by a larger decrease at 8. A single slope is a coarse summary rather than a close description of each mean.

The diagnostic plot's horizontal axis is the **fitted response**, not the factor count. Because our slope is negative, the higher-count units appear at lower fitted values, toward the left of that residual plot.

These concerns mean we should not treat the ordinary model's confidence intervals and p-values as automatically well calibrated. We can report the fitted negative trend descriptively while stating its limitations. Investigating data quality and design comes first; legitimate unusual responses should not be removed merely to obtain a desired result.

The optional extensions demonstrate a variance-robust uncertainty calculation and treating count as a category. Neither solves confounding by factor identity or establishes independence. A more detailed analysis needs a scientific plan, rather than trying methods until one produces a preferred p-value.

</details>

### Connect the two model types

With a categorical predictor, the model can give each treatment its own mean. With a numerical predictor, we restrict those means to a line. The distinction comes from the question and how the predictor is represented, not simply from the appearance of numbers in a CSV.

<details class="plan"><summary>Optional bridge: see the ANOVA as a linear model</summary>

```{r model-bridge, purl=FALSE}
group_lm <- lm(WSA ~ treatment, data = group_data)
coef(group_lm)
anova(group_lm)
```

The intercept is the control mean. The remaining coefficients estimate the other group means minus control. The overall ANOVA matches the earlier `aov()` result. The coefficient table's ordinary individual p-values are **not** a substitute for the six-pair Tukey-adjusted results.

</details>

<label class="step-check"><input type="checkbox" data-step="interpret"> I interpreted slope, units and R-squared, and recorded concerns about the line and uncertainty.</label>

## 7. Your turn: make and explain a prediction {#apply}

**Independent task · 15 minutes.** Use the provided recipe, then answer the questions in your own words. We evaluate the fitted line at the **observed factor counts**, rather than extrapolating beyond the experiment.

```{r predictions}
prediction_grid <- data.frame(Lv = c(2, 5, 8))
mean_predictions <- predict(trend_model, newdata = prediction_grid,
                            interval = "confidence", level = 0.95)
prediction_table <- data.frame(prediction_grid, mean_predictions)
prediction_table

change_8_minus_2 <- prediction_table$fit[3] - prediction_table$fit[1]
100 * change_8_minus_2
```

`predict()` evaluates the existing fitted model at the supplied counts. Its `fit` column is the fitted mean, while `lwr` and `upr` give **ordinary model-based** mean-response intervals. They inherit the limitations discussed above.

Write answers to these questions:

1. What mean mass-loss proportion does the line predict for 2 and for 8 factors?
2. What is the predicted **8-minus-2** difference in percentage points? Verify it using `6 * slope`.
3. Compare those fitted means with the observed count-level means from Part 6. Why need they not match exactly?
4. Does this fitted contrast demonstrate that adding any six factors to a given soil will cause that change? Explain using the study design.

<details class="answer"><summary>Check: predicted contrast and its scope</summary>

Fitted mean mass loss is approximately **0.659** at 2 factors, **0.637** at 5, and **0.614** at 8. The fitted 8-minus-2 contrast is about **−0.0447 proportion**, or **−4.47 percentage points**, equal to six times the fitted slope. This is a difference of percentage points, not a 4.47% relative decrease.

The observed means need not lie on the fitted line because ordinary regression chooses a line that summarises all observations, rather than a separate mean for each count. Its suitability still needs assessment.

The contrast describes this model across the sampled mixtures. Different counts contain different combinations, and we did not repeatedly add the same six factors to otherwise identical mixtures. The line does not isolate a universal factor-number effect, identify a particular driver, or estimate an interaction. The CI columns remain conditional model outputs; the diagnostics limit how confidently we should interpret their nominal coverage.

</details>

<label class="step-check"><input type="checkbox" data-step="apply"> I explained a fitted contrast in percentage points and distinguished it from a universal causal claim.</label>

## 8. Save, rerun and communicate {#save}

**Purpose:** leave a record of the data selection, model results and ecological reasoning.

The following is a supplied export recipe. It saves the complete comparison family, model-based regression intervals, predictions, data subsets and excluded IDs. You do not need to memorise the table-conversion code.

```{r save-results}
dir.create("outputs", showWarnings = FALSE)

anova_export <- data.frame(term = rownames(summary(group_model)[[1]]),
                           summary(group_model)[[1]], row.names = NULL)
trend_export <- data.frame(
  term = names(coef(trend_model)), estimate = as.numeric(coef(trend_model)),
  confint(trend_model), row.names = NULL
)
names(trend_export)[3:4] <- c("ordinary_CI_lower", "ordinary_CI_upper")
trend_export$interval_method <- "Ordinary lm; conditional on model assumptions"
trend_fit_export <- data.frame(n = nobs(trend_model), r_squared = r_squared,
                               response = "Proportional litter mass loss")
exclusions <- data.frame(
  analysis = c(rep("WSA groups", length(group_excluded_ids)),
                rep("Litter mass loss trend", length(reg_excluded_ids))),
  record_X = c(group_excluded_ids, reg_excluded_ids)
)

write.csv(group_summary, "outputs/Day4_WSA_group_summary.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(anova_export, "outputs/Day4_WSA_ANOVA.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(pairwise_table, "outputs/Day4_WSA_Tukey_all_six.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(trend_export, "outputs/Day4_trend_coefficients.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(trend_fit_export, "outputs/Day4_trend_fit.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(prediction_table, "outputs/Day4_fitted_means.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(exclusions, "outputs/Day4_excluded_records.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(group_data, "outputs/Day4_WSA_analysis_data.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(regression_data, "outputs/Day4_regression_analysis_data.csv", row.names = FALSE)

ggsave("outputs/Day4_WSA_groups.png", plot = group_plot,
       width = 7.5, height = 5, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
ggsave("outputs/Day4_litter_mass_loss_trend.png", plot = trend_plot,
       width = 7.5, height = 5.2, dpi = 300, bg = "white")

png("outputs/Day4_WSA_diagnostics.png", width = 2700, height = 1350, res = 300)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(group_model, which = 1)
plot(group_model, which = 2)
dev.off()

png("outputs/Day4_trend_diagnostics.png", width = 2700, height = 1350, res = 300)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(trend_model, which = 1)
plot(trend_model, which = 2)
dev.off()
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

### Write two short ecological interpretations

**A · Group comparison:** state the response, four groups and sample size. Explain what the overall test says, then support one control comparison with a difference and Tukey interval. State the comparison family and one diagnostic or ecological limitation.

**B · Numerical trend:** state the selected mixture counts and sample size. Report the slope in interpretable units and R-squared. Describe a model limitation visible in the data, and explain why factor identities restrict causal interpretation.

<details class="answer"><summary>Possible report structures</summary>

**A:** “We compared water-stable aggregate proportion among 45 soil units in four treatment groups. The overall ANOVA provided evidence against equal population means, conditional on the model assumptions. [Insert a control contrast, its magnitude in percentage points, and its Tukey interval.] The Tukey adjustment covered all six pairwise comparisons. [State a concern about uncertainty or evidence needed to judge ecological importance.]”

**B:** “Among 141 units with mixtures of 2, 5 or 8 factors, the fitted line associated each additional factor with about 0.745 percentage points less litter mass loss. The line accounted for about 10.3% of observed variation. [Describe the changing spread or imperfect straight-line representation.] This descriptive slope does not separate factor count from changing factor identities and combinations.”

Use your own words and distinguish conditional statistical evidence from ecological interpretation. Keep the ordinary slope interval labelled as model-based if you report it.

</details>

Save your script, choose **Session → Restart R**, and run the required analysis from its first line. Check that your files appear in `outputs` and that no objects from an earlier session are needed.

### Exit questions

1. What does an overall ANOVA establish that it cannot localise to a particular pair?
2. Why does our report retain a six-comparison adjustment when discussing three control contrasts?
3. How does treating a predictor as a factor differ from treating it as numerical?
4. What changes in your interpretation when residual spread increases along the predictor?

<details class="answer"><summary>Check your main ideas</summary>

An overall ANOVA assesses equality of the group means but does not identify the differing pairs. Our planned Tukey analysis examined all six pairs, so the reporting focus does not change that family afterward. A factor allows separate category means; the numerical term fits one straight-line slope. Increasing residual spread challenges ordinary common-variance uncertainty estimates; report the concern and investigate an appropriate analysis rather than relying only on the default p-value.

</details>

<label class="step-check"><input type="checkbox" data-step="save"> My script reruns, outputs are saved, and my two interpretations include evidence and limitations.</label>

## Optional: extend the models after the required work {#extra}

These demonstrations are additional to the three-hour route. They address different questions; they are not a sequence to try until a preferred result appears.

### A. A Welch check for the four-group question

Welch's one-way test allows unequal group variances while still comparing population means. It does not solve dependence or serious data-quality problems.

```{r optional-welch, purl=FALSE}
oneway.test(WSA ~ treatment, data = group_data, var.equal = FALSE)
```

For this selection the p-value is approximately **0.0028**, also offering evidence against a common mean under its assumptions. Do not attach the earlier Tukey intervals to this Welch analysis: those intervals came from the common-variance model. Pairwise unequal-variance inference requires a suitable, explicitly planned procedure. A question restricted to treatments versus control may also motivate a different comparison family from all six pairs.

### B. Keep the line, examine variance-robust uncertainty

Download [the supplied HC3 demonstration helper](Day4_robust_demo.R) into your project folder. The function is provided; writing it is not a learning goal today.

```{r optional-hc3, purl=FALSE}
source("Day4_robust_demo.R")
robust_trend <- robust_lm_ci(trend_model)
robust_trend
confint(trend_model)
```

HC3 changes the estimated coefficient uncertainty to allow heteroskedasticity. The helper uses **approximate t-based** intervals and p-values. Compare its slope estimate and interval with the ordinary result. The fitted line stays the same. This does not repair a wrong mean function, dependent errors, or changing factor identities; the causal interpretation remains limited.

<details class="answer"><summary>Check: does a robust interval always become wider?</summary>

No. For this example, the HC3 slope interval is approximately **−0.01112 to −0.00378**, close to the ordinary interval. A robust uncertainty calculation can produce a larger or smaller standard error. Similar results here do not remove the imperfect mean-model fit or establish a causal explanation.

</details>

### C. Allow a separate mean at each observed factor count

```{r optional-count-categories, purl=FALSE}
count_group_model <- lm(Decom ~ factor(Lv), data = regression_data)
coef(count_group_model)
anova(trend_model, count_group_model)
```

The categorical model allows separate means at 2, 5 and 8. The numerical model restricts those means to a line. The nested comparison evaluates that restriction under ordinary linear-model error assumptions, using the same observations. Its classical p-value is itself subject to the variance concerns already seen; it is not an automatic model-selection rule. Begin with the scientific question and the observed mean pattern.

### D. Add a second predictor: factor dissimilarity

The supplied `dissim` index describes how dissimilar a mixture's component factors were based on single-factor response profiles. The study normalised the index **within factor-count levels**. A value of 0.8 is therefore a relative position on that provided scale, not a universal raw distance or a literal percentage of biological difference.

We fit **additive predictor terms** with `+`. This does not include a statistical interaction term. Creating and interpreting interactions is a later topic.

```{r optional-multiple-regression, purl=FALSE}
multiple_keep <- complete.cases(regression_data[, c("Decom", "Lv", "dissim")])
multiple_data <- regression_data[multiple_keep, ]
nrow(multiple_data)

count_only <- lm(Decom ~ Lv, data = multiple_data)
count_and_dissim <- lm(Decom ~ Lv + dissim, data = multiple_data)

summary(count_and_dissim)
confint(count_and_dissim)
anova(count_only, count_and_dissim)

model_fit_table <- data.frame(
  model = c("Count only", "Count plus dissimilarity"),
  n = c(nobs(count_only), nobs(count_and_dissim)),
  R_squared = c(summary(count_only)$r.squared,
                summary(count_and_dissim)$r.squared),
  adjusted_R_squared = c(summary(count_only)$adj.r.squared,
                         summary(count_and_dissim)$adj.r.squared)
)
model_fit_table
```

**Do:** explain the `dissim` coefficient as a fitted association **holding numerical count constant**. Why must the nested models use the same observations? Does a larger in-sample R-squared demonstrate better predictions for new soil units?

<details class="answer"><summary>Check: a conditional association, not a causal explanation</summary>

Both models use **141 rows** here. The dissimilarity coefficient is approximately **−0.081** per whole index unit, or about **−0.81 percentage points** for a 0.1 index increase at the same count under this additive line model. The Lv coefficient also changes when the second predictor is added.

The models need the same response observations for this nested comparison. R-squared increases from about **0.103 to 0.225** in the fitted data; adding a predictor cannot reduce ordinary R-squared. Adjusted R-squared accounts for parameter count, but neither metric establishes held-out predictive performance. We will revisit prediction on Day 5.

The dissimilarity index comes from single-factor effect profiles, and this simple model does not control all factor identities or separate mechanisms. Its association should not be presented as an isolated causal dissimilarity effect. The original study used a more detailed analysis; today's extension teaches model interpretation. Residual/design checks still apply.

</details>

## Help, downloads and references {#help}

<details class="plan"><summary>Something did not run?</summary>

- **File not found:** extract the ZIP, open its project, then check `getwd()`, `list.files()` and `file.exists("MultiFactor_data.csv")`.
- **Object not found:** run earlier required commands in order. R is case-sensitive; `Lv` and `lv` are different names.
- **Package missing:** install `ggplot2` once and load it in every new session. Core work needs no `emmeans`, `car`, `broom`, `GGally` or `tidyverse` installation.
- **Wrong treatment counts:** select the explicit remark labels CT, D, H, S. Do not select the first four values returned by `unique()`.
- **Unexpected regression slope:** verify the response and subset. This lesson selects only Lv 2, 5 and 8, then complete Decom/Lv records; an all-row fit answers a different question.
- **A strange missingness count:** inspect only variables needed for the current model. Do not apply `na.omit()` to every column of the original data frame.
- **Tukey output is missing:** run `aov()` on the factor `treatment` before `TukeyHSD()`. The spelling and capital letters matter.
- **Factor versus number:** `str()` checks how R stored the variable. The category names and the scientific question determine how it should enter the model; a numerical-looking label is not automatically a numerical trend.
- **Several diagnostic plot windows:** run `par(mfrow = c(1, 1))` after the paired plots. Saving figures to PNG does not change the original data.

</details>

**Data and research context:** the CSV is unchanged from the supplied Day 4 course file. The teaching selections and ordinary models are simplified exercises. See Bi et al. (2024), [*Number and dissimilarity of global change factors influences soil properties and functions*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-52511-2), for the original study design, measurements and fuller analysis.

**R references:** [ANOVA with `aov()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/aov.html), [Tukey comparisons](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/TukeyHSD.html), [fitting linear models](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/lm.html), [mean-response and prediction intervals](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/predict.lm.html), [Welch's one-way test](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/oneway.test.html), and [comparing nested models](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/anova.lm.html).
